processing: Handled as Yunnan raw pu-erh usually is: wilted, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then pressed or kept loose, with no ripening pile.
harvest_season: As across Mengku, spring is the most sought-after picking.
appearance_dry: Long dark green strips of large leaf, typical of Mengku raw tea.
appearance_wet: Thick, supple large leaves in olive to yellow-green.
taste_profile: Described as sugary and wild-honey sweet with mountain florals, a soft full body and a long, strong returning sweetness.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan and short steeps; the returning sweetness is reported to grow over the session, so do not stop after two or three infusions.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, either as loose mao cha or pressed cakes, with single-year cakes such as 2019 and 2020 productions on the Western market. Young spring tea is the bulk of what you will see. Like other raw pu-erh it can be drunk young or stored; older examples are few because the village name is a recent selling point.
description:
Zhengqitang is a small village at around 2000 metres on the Dongbanshan, the eastern half of the Mengku tea area in Shuangjiang County. Its selling point is a nickname: 'little Bingdao', for a sweetness people compare with the famous village across the valley.

The tea is Mengku large-leaf picked from older village gardens and made in the usual raw pu-erh way. The altitude and the trees shape the cup more than any special method does.

Tea drinkers describe sugary, wild-honey notes in the dry leaf, high florals in the cup, a soft full body and a returning sweetness that builds as the session goes on. These notes come mostly from sellers and enthusiasts. Brew hot and short, as you would other strong Mengku raw teas.

It is sold by year and costs far less than Bingdao; one list of spring prices had old-tree Zhengqitang at 600 to 800 yuan per kilo. 'Little Bingdao' is a marketing phrase also applied to other villages, so judge the tea, not the slogan.
history:
The village was once inhabited by Lahu people, who left dozens of acres of tea gardens with trunks grown thicker than a big bowl. In 1903 the Lahu moved away and Han settlers took over and planted more tea. The old name was reportedly Zhangqitang, 'miasma pond', changed that same year to the present 'righteous energy pond'.

Its location helped trade: people could walk to the Boshang market in about three hours, or leave tea at the door for passing horse caravans. Little more is documented about the tea itself.
